intro.html: Low energy has many shades. Someone may be unwilling to work, too tired to try, slow and dreamy on a hot day, half asleep, or fast asleep. Writers use these words to set a mood (a languid summer afternoon) or to judge a person (an indolent worker).

Won’t make an effort: indolent. Low on energy: lethargic, languid, listless, torpid, and the feeling lassitude. Sleepy and asleep: somnolent (drowsy), soporific (causing sleep), dormant (sleeping for now), stupor (a dazed state).
Several come from Latin words for sleep: somn (somnolent, insomnia), sopor (soporific) and dorm (dormant, dormitory).

words.def: lazy; unwilling to work or make an effort
words.ex: The {indolent} cat watched the mouse run past without even lifting its head.
words.ctx: Though he was clever, the {indolent} student never finished an assignment, preferring to nap in the library rather than do any work at all.
words.etym: From Late Latin indolens, “feeling no pain”: in- (not) + dolere (to suffer); in English it came to mean “not troubling oneself,” and so lazy.

mn.text: The chore list grows longer every day, but Jonah stays sprawled on the sofa, too idle to lift a finger: he is {indolent}.

scene.alt: A teen lies on the sofa ignoring a sign that lists his chores and a broom left leaning nearby.

words.ex: The heat made everyone {lethargic}, and no one wanted to play outside.
words.ctx: After the long overnight flight, the travelers were {lethargic}; they shuffled slowly through the airport, yawning and barely speaking.
words.etym: From Greek lethargos, “forgetful, drowsy”: lethe (forgetting) + argos (idle).

mn.text: The monkey bounces around shouting “Come and play!”, but the sloth just groans, “Argh… later.” The sloth is {lethargic}.

scene.alt: A sleepy sloth hangs from a branch, groaning, while a lively monkey bounces nearby.

words.def: slow, relaxed and without energy, often in a graceful way
words.ex: We spent a {languid} afternoon floating on the lake.
words.ctx: Unlike his brisk, busy sister, Felix moved with {languid} ease, strolling rather than walking and taking twice as long to do everything.
words.etym: From Latin languidus, “faint, weak,” from languere (to be weak).

mn.text: On a hot afternoon, the cat stretches out long on the sunny bench and moves only to flick her tail: she is {languid}.

scene.alt: A cat stretches out lazily on a sunny park bench.

words.ex: Without its morning walk, the dog lay {listless} by the door.
words.ctx: The team looked {listless} in the second half, missing easy passes and barely chasing the ball, as if all their energy had drained away.
words.etym: From list, an old word for desire or wish, + -less (without).

mn.cue: LIST-LESS: no wish to do a thing
mn.text: When the big game is called off, Lila slumps on the floor with her to-do list still blank; she has no wish to do anything at all. She is {listless}.

scene.alt: A girl slumps on her bedroom floor with a blank to-do list and an unused ball.

words.def: slow and inactive, as if numb
words.ex: In the cold, the {torpid} lizard barely moved.
words.ctx: The village seemed {torpid} in the summer heat; shops closed at noon, dogs slept in the shade, and nothing stirred until evening.
words.etym: From Latin torpidus, from torpere (to be numb).

mn.text: On a frosty morning, the tortoise hardly moves at all until the sun warms its shell: it is {torpid}.

scene.alt: A tortoise sits frozen still on a frosty morning, waiting for the sun to warm it.

words.def: sleepy and drowsy; ready to doze off
words.ex: The {somnolent} passengers dozed as the train rocked along.
words.ctx: By the third hour of the meeting, the room had grown {somnolent}: heads drooped, eyes closed, and someone began, very softly, to snore.

mn.cue: SOMN = sleep: drowsy on the train
mn.text: On the long ride home, Rosa’s head keeps nodding toward her shoulder, and her eyes won’t stay open: she is {somnolent}.

scene.alt: Two travelers nod off on a station bench.

words.ex: The speaker’s {soporific} voice put half the class to sleep.
words.ctx: The gentle rain on the roof had a {soporific} effect; within minutes of lying down, every camper in the tent was fast asleep.

mn.cue: SOUP-orific: soup that makes you SLEEPY
mn.text: Nana Lou’s warm soup is so soothing that after one bowl, Grandpa and Kai both nod off at the table: the soup is {soporific}.

scene.alt: A grandfather and a boy fall asleep at the table next to a pot of warm soup.

words.def: asleep or inactive for a time, but able to wake again
words.ex: The {dormant} volcano has not erupted for three hundred years.
words.ctx: Seeds can stay {dormant} in the soil all winter, waiting until the warm spring rains wake them and they begin to sprout.
words.etym: From French dormant, “sleeping,” from dormir (to sleep), from Latin dormire.
words.note: Dormant means asleep for now, not dead: a dormant volcano can erupt again.

mn.cue: DORM-ant: asleep, but it will WAKE
mn.text: All winter the bear sleeps under the snow, quiet and still, but in spring it will wake up hungry: through the winter it is {dormant}.

scene.alt: A bear sleeps through the winter as snow falls around it.

words.def: a heavy tiredness of body or mind
words.ex: A strange {lassitude} came over him after the long trip.
words.ctx: Weeks of hard work left Maya with a deep {lassitude}; even simple tasks like answering a letter felt like climbing a mountain.

mn.text: After a week of exams and late nights, the lass drags her heavy backpack home, weary in every bone: she is full of {lassitude}.

scene.alt: A weary teen girl drags herself home under a heavy backpack.

words.def: a dazed state in which one can hardly think or act
words.ex: Woken at five in the morning, Dev stumbled around in a {stupor}.
words.ctx: The news of the surprise win left the coach in a happy {stupor}; she stood on the sideline, blinking, unable to say a word.
words.etym: From Latin stupor, “numbness, amazement,” from stupere (to be stunned).

mn.text: Half asleep at dawn, Dev stoops over the table and pours orange juice onto his cereal: he is in a {stupor}.

scene.alt: A sleepy teen in a daze pours orange juice into his cereal bowl.

after.cap: Who is sleepy, and what makes them so.

after.html: soporific describes what causes sleep (a soporific lecture). somnolent describes the one who is sleepy (a somnolent student). A boring speech is soporific; the people listening become somnolent.

after.name: vo-cloze

opts.s: The hum of the old fan was so {soporific} that Grandpa fell asleep in his chair.

after.cap: The fan causes sleep, so it is soporific.

items.q: Which phrase uses the right word?
items.why: A lullaby causes sleep, so it is soporific. The yawning baby would be somnolent.

items.q: True or false: a dormant volcano can never erupt again.
items.why: False. Dormant means asleep for now. A dormant volcano is quiet, but it can wake.

items.q: Which word blames a person for not wanting to work?
items.why: Indolent means lazy, avoiding effort. Somnolent only means sleepy, which may not be anyone’s fault.

items.q: Type the word built on the Latin somn (sleep) that means drowsy.
